propositions.text: The appellant is a Vietnamese citizen appealing the RPD's November 29, 2019 decision rejecting her refugee claim.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Vietnam. She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated November 29, 2019, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant is a Vietnamese citizen appealing the RPD's November 29, 2019 decision rejecting her refugee claim, says the court.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed; the RPD was correct that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The key issues are credibility and availability of an internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: The determinative issues in this appeal are credibility and the availability of an internal flight alternative (IFA).

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, finding the RPD correct on refugee status and protection, focusing on credibility and IFA issues.

propositions.text: The appellant alleges fear of her abusive, criminal husband and multiple failed escape attempts.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges a fear of her husband, whom she married in 2008, and who is a womanizing, gambling, drug addicted criminal... The Appellant alleges that her husband beat her frequently during their marriage... The Appellant alleges to have escaped from her husband on three occasions, in 2011, 2013, and in 2016.

propositions.text: She fled to Ho Chi Minh City in 2016 and later came to Canada, claiming refugee protection after a work permit denial.
propositions.quote: She took that opportunity to go back to the airport and flee to Ho Chi Minh City, where she remained in hiding until she received her Canadian visa... and made a claim for refugee protection on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, after her application for a work permit was denied.

propositions.text: Her husband continues to harass her parents in Vietnam.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that her husband continues to harass her parents.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleges abuse and failed escapes from her husband, fled to Ho Chi Minh City, then Canada, and claims ongoing harassment of her parents, says appellant.

propositions.text: The court's role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD's decision was correct.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD's decision was correct.

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant was in an abusive relationship but had a viable IFA in Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: The RPD accepted that the Appellant was in an abusive domestic relationship, but also determined that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Ho Chi Minh City and that it would not be unreasonable for her to relocate there.

propositions.text: The appellant argues the RPD erred; cities are not large and husband would find her due to her youth and care for him.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that this was an erroneous finding, that Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are not as large as they sound, and that the Appellant's husband would be motivated to find her because she is young and could care for him.

propositions.text: After independent analysis, the court finds a viable IFA exists in Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: After conducting an independent analysis, I too find that there is a viable IFA for the Appellant in Ho Chi Minh City.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found an abusive relationship but viable IFA; appellant argues error; court independently finds viable IFA in Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: FCA in Rasaratnam sets a two-prong test for IFA: no serious persecution possibility and unreasonableness of seeking refuge there.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), in Rasaratnam,2 provides that the test to be applied in determining whether there is an IFA is two-pronged: (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists. (2) And the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The FCA's Rasaratnam test requires no serious persecution risk and unreasonableness of seeking refuge for IFA determination, explains prior court.

propositions.text: FCA in Thirunavukkarasu sets a high threshold for unreasonableness; hardship from relocation alone is insufficient.
propositions.quote: The FCA went on to provide guidance with respect to the "unreasonableness test" in the second prong of the test in Thirunavukkarasu.3 It spelled out a very high threshold regarding what makes an IFA unreasonable in all of the circumstances. Hardship that is associated with dislocation and relocation is not one that would render an IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: Appellant must prove adverse conditions jeopardizing life and safety in the IFA location.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is required to provide proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize her life and safety in travelling to and in living in the IFA location.

paragraphs.summary: The FCA in Thirunavukkarasu requires a high threshold for unreasonableness; hardship alone insufficient; appellant must prove life-jeopardizing conditions.

propositions.text: Both prongs of the IFA test must be satisfied; onus shifts to appellant to prove no IFA once raised.
propositions.quote: For the Appellant to have an IFA, both prongs of the test must be satisfied. The onus shifts to the Appellant to prove that she does not have an IFA once the issue has been raised and potential IFAs have been proposed.

propositions.text: Is there a serious possibility of persecution in Ho Chi Minh City?
propositions.quote: Is there a serious possibility of persecution in Ho Chi Minh City?

paragraphs.summary: The court states both IFA test prongs must be met; onus shifts to appellant; asks if serious persecution risk exists in Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: Vietnam is populous (~100 million) with large land mass; Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have ~8 and ~9 million people respectively.
propositions.quote: According to the World Fact Book,4 Vietnam is the world's 15th most populous nation with a population approaching 100 million as of July 2017. The country has a land mass of over 330,000 square kilometres. The capital city of Hanoi has a population approaching eight million, and Ho Chi Minh City has a population of almost nine million.

paragraphs.summary: The World Fact Book shows Vietnam is populous with large cities Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, says the court.

propositions.text: RPD accepted abusive relationship but found insufficient evidence husband could locate appellant throughout Vietnam or motivated to do so.
propositions.quote: The RPD accepted that the Appellant was in an abusive domestic relationship. The RPD also determined that there was insufficient evidence that the Appellant's husband has the ability or access to information that would result in him being able to locate the Appellant throughout Vietnam. Further, the RPD determined that the husband was not motivated to continue to locate her if she lived elsewhere in Vietnam.

propositions.text: Appellant argues husband could find her via extensive network and is motivated due to her youth.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that her husband would be able to find her through his extensive network and that her age distinguishes her from his previous wives in terms of his motivation to pursue her.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found insufficient evidence husband could locate or motivated to find appellant; appellant argues otherwise, says court.

propositions.text: Once IFA identified, onus shifts to appellant to prove serious persecution risk if she relocates there.
propositions.quote: Once an IFA is identified, the onus shifts to the Appellant to establish that a serious possibility of persecution or risk of danger exists if she were to locate there.

propositions.text: The appellant's husband would not locate her if she relocated to Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant's husband would not locate her if she were to travel to Ho Chi Minh City.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds onus shifts to appellant to prove persecution risk; finds husband would not locate her in Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: Appellant described husband as gang leader in Haiphong with no evidence of connections outside that city.
propositions.quote: A review of the record shows that the Appellant described her husband as a leader of a gang in her home city of Haiphong, who extorted money from local businesses.

propositions.text: No evidence husband had extensive network or business outside Haiphong.
propositions.quote: The record reveals no evidence of the husband having any connections or business outside of Haiphong, and no evidence whatsoever that he had an extensive network as the Appellant argues.

propositions.text: It is not credible that husband's staff randomly found appellant in Hanoi, a large city, without evidence of connections there.
propositions.quote: I do not find it credible, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's husband's staff, for whom there is no evidence of having any connections outside of Haiphong, would randomly locate her in front of her apartment, in a city of almost eight million people, in a country that is over 300,000 square kilometres large, and has a population approaching 100 million.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no evidence husband had network outside Haiphong and did not credibly find appellant in Hanoi, says court.

propositions.text: Appellant argues Haiphong people are tightly connected and husband followed parents to Hanoi.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also argues that the reason her husband's underlings found her in Hanoi is because people of Haiphong are often tightly connected and in touch with each other wherever they might be currently living.

propositions.text: This is speculation without evidence; appellant had only one friend in Hanoi, no evidence of other contacts or husband following parents.
propositions.quote: This is mere speculation; the Appellant has not provided any evidence to support this cultural practice... There is no other evidence that she was in touch with any persons from Haiphong as the Appellant asserts. Further, there is no evidence to support the Appellant's argument that her husband somehow followed her parents to Hanoi when they were bringing her supplies.

propositions.text: Appellant did not credibly establish she was located by husband or fled to Hanoi in 2011.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not credibly established that she was located by her husband or that she fled to Hanoi in 2011.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's argument about Haiphong connections and husband's following parents speculative and not credible.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges fleeing husband in 2013 to Ho Chi Minh City then Hanoi, found and returned to Haiphong.
propositions.quote: In 2013, the Appellant alleged that she once again fled her husband. She testified that she flew to Ho Chi Minh City... and remained there for two weeks until a neighbour called her to tell her that her husband was flying there, so she flew to Hanoi a second time, and remained there for two more weeks until she was again found.

propositions.text: Neighbour did not know appellant was in Ho Chi Minh City and called on a phone number she did not have; this is not credible.
propositions.quote: The evidence suggests that the neighbour did not have the new phone number of the Appellant. I do not find it credible that a neighbour would call the Appellant on a phone number she did not have, in a city she did not know the Appellant was in, to tell her that her husband was flying to that very same city to look for her.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony about who found her in Hanoi is inconsistent, undermining credibility of 2013 escape claim.
propositions.quote: In her narrative the Appellant states that she was found in Hanoi by her husband and his underlings and dragged back to Haiphong. In her testimony the Appellant stated that her husband alone came to her place to find her. This inconsistency in her evidence impugns the Appellant's allegation that she escaped and was located in 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's 2013 escape story not credible due to inconsistent testimony and implausible neighbour call.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges fleeing husband in 2016 at airport, deceived him to escape to Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: In 2016, the Appellant alleges to have fled once again... She was able, ultimately, to flee back to the airport and onwards to Ho Chi Minh City again, simply by asking her husband to let her go have her hair done for a wedding they were to attend that night.

propositions.text: The explanation is not credible given prior restrictions and prior escape attempts; husband unlikely to allow her to leave.
propositions.quote: I do not find this to be a reasonable explanation... it is not credible, on a balance, that he would just allow her to go get her hair done, and thus be able to flee to Ho Chi Minh City.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's 2016 escape explanation not credible given prior restrictions and husband's behavior.

propositions.text: Appellant did not list addresses in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City in forms despite living there; her explanation is not credible.
propositions.quote: Further, despite living in Hanoi in a rented apartment for three weeks in 2011, living in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi for one month in 2013... the Appellant never listed these addresses in her forms... This is not a credible reply.

propositions.text: Appellant has not credibly established she escaped to Ho Chi Minh City in 2016.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not credibly established that she escaped to Ho Chi Minh City in 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's failure to list addresses undermines credibility of 2016 escape claim.

propositions.text: Appellant testified husband continues to harass her parents, requiring cameras at their home.
propositions.quote: Also, the Appellant testified that her husband continues to harass her parents in Vietnam regarding her return, so much so that she and her sister had to have cameras installed at their parents' home.

propositions.text: Parents' letter describes one incident of husband's visit that angered them.
propositions.quote: This is inconsistent with a letter from the Appellant's parents who outline one instance of her husband visiting them and that this had angered them.

propositions.text: Court prefers parents' letter over appellant's testimony about ongoing harassment.
propositions.quote: I prefer the evidence of the parents, who are describing in their own words their interaction with and feelings about their son-in-law.

paragraphs.summary: The court prefers parents' letter over appellant's testimony about ongoing harassment by husband.

propositions.text: Husband visited parents only once in three years; no evidence of ongoing harassment or efforts to move parents away.
propositions.quote: Her parents live on the other side of the riverbank from her husband, yet in the three years since she left Vietnam her husband has only gone to her parents' home once to look for her... absence of any efforts to move her parents away from her husband.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD mischaracterized lack of financial means to sponsor parents to Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that this was a mischaracterization, that the Appellant's sister simply did not have the finances to sponsor her parents to come to Canada.

propositions.text: Appellant argues parents could not move within Vietnam due to police revealing address to husband.
propositions.quote: Also, the evidence does not support the Appellant's assertion that her parents could not move within Vietnam because in so doing they would have to reveal their new address to the local police, and by extension to her husband given his connection to the police.

propositions.text: Court finds no evidence husband connected to police; no harassment demonstrated; undermines appellant's claim husband motivated to find her via parents.
propositions.quote: There is no mention in the record of her husband having any connection to the police... I find that, on a balance, the evidence does not demonstrate that the Appellant's parents continue to be harassed by her husband, and this undermines the Appellant's allegations that her husband is motivated to find her via her parents.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of ongoing harassment or police connection; appellant's arguments about finances and moving unsupported.

propositions.text: Appellant has not established husband has motivation or means to locate her in Ho Chi Minh City; no serious persecution risk there.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that her husband has the motivation and means to locate her in Ho Chi Minh City. I find that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: Is it unreasonable for appellant to relocate to Ho Chi Minh City?
propositions.quote: Is it unreasonable, in all the circumstances, for the Appellant to relocate to Ho Chi Minh City?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious persecution risk in Ho Chi Minh City and asks if relocation there is unreasonable.

propositions.text: RPD found it reasonable for appellant to seek refuge in Ho Chi Minh City after reviewing evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD, after reviewing the objective documentary evidence, determined it is reasonable for the Appellant to seek refuge in Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: Appellant has not contested RPD's finding on reasonableness of relocation.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not contested this finding.

propositions.text: Court finds RPD's determination correct; appellant has not shown undue hardship in relocating to Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD determination was correct and the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she would face undue hardship in relocation to Ho Chi Minh City.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's reasonableness finding correct; appellant does not show undue hardship relocating to Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: The RPD took into account Chairperson's Guideline 4 on women refugee claimants fearing gender-related persecution.
propositions.quote: The RPD, in its decision, states that it took into account the contents of the Chairperson's Guideline 4 - Women refugee claimants fearing gender related persecution.

propositions.text: The RPD considered social, economic, and cultural factors and country condition evidence from the National Documentation Package (NDP).
propositions.quote: In doing so, the RPD considered various social, economic, and cultural factors. Similarly, the RPD states that it considered the country condition evidence which is contained in the National Documentation Package (NDP).

propositions.text: Independent analysis shows women in Vietnam can do most things independently with few restrictions, including single or divorced women living alone.
propositions.quote: An independent analysis of the objective country evidence shows that women in Vietnam can do most things on their own with very few restrictions, and there are no restrictions on single or divorced women living alone.

propositions.text: Cultural tendencies against women living alone are changing, especially in larger cities where neighbors do not know each other.
propositions.quote: The same evidence indicates that although women who live alone are generally poorly perceived, these cultural tendencies are changing and that in larger cities where neighbours do not know one another that is not the situation.

propositions.text: Women and men can relocate freely in Vietnam; relocation is easier for women in large cities like Hanoi; educated women have advantages in work and housing.
propositions.quote: The evidence suggests that women and men can relocate freely in Vietnam, but it is easier for women to relocate in large cities like Hanoi, and that educated women have an advantage at finding work and accommodations.

propositions.text: The appellant is an educated woman who completed high school in Vietnam.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is an educated woman, having completed high school in Vietnam.

propositions.text: The appellant has significant experience as a nail technician in Canada and Vietnam and has family support.
propositions.quote: She has significant experience as a nail technician both in Canada and in Vietnam, and continues to have the support of her sister and her parents.

propositions.text: The appellant will be able to support herself in Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant will be able to support herself in Ho Chi Minh City.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD considered Guideline 4 and country evidence; the court finds women in Vietnam have few restrictions, the appellant is educated and supported, and can support herself in Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: The appellant can travel to the IFA in Ho Chi Minh City, which has an international airport and direct travel access.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has the ability to travel to the IFA in Ho Chi Minh City. It is serviced by an international airport, and she could travel there directly.

propositions.text: The appellant has traveled to Ho Chi Minh City at least three times and lived there in 2016 with a friend while awaiting her visa.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has travelled to Ho Chi Minh City on at least three occasions and remained there in 2016, living with a friend while awaiting her visa.

propositions.text: The appellant has previously relocated to Hong Kong and Canada.
propositions.quote: I also note that the Appellant has also previously relocated to Hong Kong and Canada.

propositions.text: The appellant could reasonably relocate to Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: As a result, I find that she could reasonably relocate to Ho Chi Minh City.

propositions.text: The appellant did not identify any factors other than fear of her husband that would limit or cause undue hardship in relocating to Ho Chi Minh City.
propositions.quote: The record also shows that the Appellant did not identify any factors, other than those relating to the fear of her husband, that would limit her ability to relocate to or cause her any undue hardship in relocating to Ho Chi Minh City.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant can travel and reasonably relocate to Ho Chi Minh City, with no limiting factors except fear of her husband.

propositions.text: A viable internal flight alternative (IFA) exists for the appellant.
propositions.quote: Based upon all the evidence, I find that a viable IFA does exist for the Appellant.

propositions.text: There is no serious possibility the appellant would be persecuted if returned to Vietnam under section 96 IRPA.
propositions.quote: I find that there is not a serious possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted if she returned to Vietnam, pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: On a balance of probabilities, the appellant would not face danger of torture, risk to life, or cruel and unusual treatment under section 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: I also find, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Vietnam, pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a viable IFA exists and no serious risk of persecution, torture, or cruel treatment for the appellant in Vietnam.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed and the RPD decision is confirmed that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee protection to the appellant.
